h1: Which SEO tool is best for your actual situation
metaTitle: Which SEO Tool Is Best? Depends on the Job
metaDescription: Which SEO tool is best depends on the job: crawling, keywords or links. Here's the pick for each, plus why most small sites should pay for nothing yet.
answer: There isn't one. The best crawler, the best link index and the best keyword database are three different products, and Search Console beats all of them for data about your own site. For most small Indian sites, the honest answer for the first six months is no paid tool at all.
takeaways: Buy per job. A crawler answers a question no keyword suite can, and vice versa — the all-in-one suites are strong at two of the six jobs and adequate at the rest.
Search Console covers your own site better than any paid product, because it isn't estimating. It's blind to three specific things, and those three are what you're actually buying.
Annual billing typically saves about the price of two months. That's a bad deal on a tool you open twice a quarter.
**A subscription is premature until someone has hours free to act on what it reports.** Otherwise you've bought a better description of the problem.

body: Every comparison article answers this by picking a winner, because a winner is easier to write than a decision framework. It's also wrong, in a specific and expensive way.

SEO tools aren't competing products with different feature lists. They're different databases. A crawler builds a picture of your site by walking it. A link tool crawls the web continuously and records which page points at which. A keyword tool stores query data with modelled volumes. Asking which is best is like asking whether a microscope beats a map.

The all-in-one suites blur this because they sell all three at once. They're genuinely strong at keyword and link data and merely fine at crawling — which is why agencies that own a suite still buy a separate crawler. Nobody advertises that.
There are no affiliate links anywhere on this page, which is worth saying because most articles ranking for this query are paid by the answer they give.

sections.h2: Where the paid tools genuinely differ — and where they don't
body: Three real differences justify the money, and two heavily marketed ones don't.

**Real: the size and freshness of the link index.** This is the one thing you cannot approximate. A tool that recrawls the web faster shows you a new link days sooner and finds links smaller indexes miss entirely. If link analysis is your job, this is what you're paying for and it's worth paying for.
**Real: competitor keyword visibility.** Seeing every query a rival ranks for, with their landing pages, is unavailable free at any scale. It's the single most common reason to start a subscription.

**Real: historical data.** Position history, link history, page-level trends going back years. Useful for diagnosing why traffic fell in March, and impossible to reconstruct after the fact — which is also why switching trackers costs you your history.
**Not real: search volume accuracy.** Every provider models it, and two tools disagreeing by 3x on the same phrase is routine. Don't choose on this.

**Not real: difficulty scores.** Each is a proprietary number derived mostly from links. Fine for sorting a list, meaningless as an absolute, and not comparable between tools. Two suites that both say 'KD 42' aren't agreeing about anything. The suites are more alike than their marketing suggests, which we've picked apart in [Ahrefs vs Semrush](/compare/ahrefs-vs-semrush).

callout.title: Don't buy a tool to answer a question you haven't asked
callout.body: Write down the three questions you need answered this quarter before you open a pricing page. If the answer to all three is in Search Console, close the tab. If two of them are about competitors, you have a real reason to subscribe — and you now know which tier you need.

sections.h2: What Search Console already does, and the three things it can't
body: Search Console is the best SEO tool available and it costs nothing, because Google is reporting its own data rather than estimating someone else's. Sixteen months of every query you appeared for, with clicks, impressions and average position. Index status for every URL. A live rendering test that shows exactly what Googlebot received. Your external links. Core Web Vitals from real users.
For a site under a few hundred pages, that answers most of the questions anyone will ask you in a year. So be precise about what's missing, because those gaps are the actual product you'd be buying.
numbered: **It shows nothing about competitors.** No rival's keywords, no rival's links, no view of who's gaining on you. This is the main reason people pay.

**It can't show queries you've never appeared for.** If you rank nowhere for a term, it doesn't exist in your reports. Discovering demand you haven't earned needs a different source — and much of that is [free anyway](/answers/where-to-find-keywords-for-seo).

**It doesn't crawl your site.** It reports on URLs Google found; it won't tell you that 60 pages have duplicate titles or that a section has no internal links pointing into it. That's a crawler's job.

sections.h2: What it costs in rupees, and whether annual billing pays
body: Most of these tools price in dollars or pounds, so your rupee cost moves with the exchange rate, and every vendor reshuffles tiers periodically. The bands below are for planning; check the current page before you commit.

Entry tiers of the major suites land somewhere around ₹9,000–₹14,000 a month once converted. Budget suites sit nearer ₹2,500–₹4,500. A desktop crawler licence is an annual charge that works out to roughly ₹1,500–₹2,500 a month when spread across the year, and it's the best value on the list.

On annual billing: most suites discount it by roughly the price of two months. That's a real saving if the tool is central to how you work every week. It's a trap if you're buying it for a project — a twelve-month commitment on a tool you open in March and forget by May costs more than the monthly plan you'd have cancelled in April.

The rule we'd give a founder: pay monthly for the first three months of any tool. If you've opened it in week one, week five and week ten without being reminded to, switch to annual and take the discount. If you haven't, cancel and keep the ₹1,20,000 a year.

callout.title: One subscription, shared properly
callout.body: Most suite licences limit seats and treat sharing as a terms violation, so the honest way to run this on a small team is one paid seat for whoever does the research, with everyone else on Search Console and Looker Studio. Those are unlimited, free, and cover what the rest of the team actually needs.

sections.h2: When a tool subscription is premature
body: This is the part the comparison articles won't tell you, for obvious commercial reasons.
For most Indian sites under a hundred pages, spending nothing on tools for six months is the correct decision. Not the frugal one — the correct one. Here's the test.
bullets: **You aren't publishing yet.** A keyword tool on a site that ships one page a quarter is a subscription to a list of things you won't do. Fix the publishing cadence first.
**Nobody has hours free.** A suite generates hundreds of findings a week. If there's no one with time to implement, the tool converts your problem into a longer document about your problem.

**Search Console still has unexploited data.** If you haven't worked through your position 8–20 queries, you have unbanked wins sitting in a free tool. Do those first — they're faster than anything a new subscription will surface.

**Your technical basics are unchecked.** Run the free crawler tier over 500 URLs. If it finds duplicate titles, broken links and orphaned pages, you have a quarter of work already, and none of it needs a paid product.
**You're buying it to look professional.** Fair enough, but a Looker Studio dashboard on free data looks equally professional and costs nothing.

sections.h2: How we'd spend the first ₹10,000 a month
body: In order, stopping when the budget runs out or the need does.

**₹0 — Search Console, GA4, Looker Studio, Screaming Frog free tier.** Set up properly, verified on every property variant, with the sitemap submitted. Most sites never complete this step, which is why it's first.
**₹1,500–₹2,500 a month — a crawler licence**, once your site exceeds 500 URLs. It answers structural questions nothing free can, and it's an annual charge rather than a recurring drip.
**₹2,500–₹4,500 a month — a budget keyword suite**, when you have a publishing plan and need competitor keyword lists to prioritise it. Not before the plan exists.
**The rest — writing.** At Indian rates the remaining budget buys a couple of genuinely good pages a month, and pages are the thing that ranks. Tools have never ranked anything.

If you'd rather not assemble any of this, it's part of what our [SEO work](/seo) covers — including the unglamorous fact that tool spend is the smallest line in a plan that works. All of it gets measured against one number: your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic, frozen the day we start. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it.

faqs.q: What is the single best SEO tool?
faqs.a: Google Search Console, if you only get one — it reports Google's own data about your site rather than estimating it, and it's free. Once you need data about sites you don't own, the question splits by job: a crawler for structure, a link index for authority, a keyword database for demand.

faqs.q: Ahrefs or Semrush for a beginner?
faqs.a: Either. For a beginner the difference that matters isn't the data, it's which interface you'll actually open weekly. Ahrefs is generally regarded as stronger on link data; Semrush covers more ground including paid search. Trial both on monthly billing and keep whichever one you used unprompted.

faqs.q: What's the best free SEO tool?
faqs.a: Search Console, and it isn't close. Second place goes to Screaming Frog's free tier for crawling up to 500 URLs, which answers structural questions Search Console won't touch. Between those two, plus Google Trends and Keyword Planner, a small site is genuinely well equipped for ₹0.

faqs.q: Is a ₹12,000 a month SEO tool worth it for a small business?
faqs.a: Usually not in year one. That's roughly ₹1,44,000 annually, which buys a meaningful amount of writing at Indian rates, and pages rank while dashboards don't. The subscription earns its keep when you're competing hard enough that competitor data changes what you publish next.

faqs.q: Should I pay annually to get the discount?
faqs.a: Only after three months of monthly billing prove you use it. The typical annual discount is around the price of two months, which is real money if the tool is part of your weekly routine and wasted money if it turns out to be a project purchase you'd have cancelled in April.

faqs.q: Do AI SEO tools replace the traditional ones?
faqs.a: Not yet. Most sit on the same underlying data and add a generation layer — drafting the brief or the title rather than just flagging the gap. Genuinely useful for speed. They don't decide what's worth publishing, and they can't tell you whether the page you shipped earned a lead.
